utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Could the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. If you could take a seat and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I am Grgo Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we discussed, part of your evidence in this case is going to be submitted in writing and we need to deal with the formalities related to that submission first. You testified in the Brdjanin trial in June in 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've subsequently had an opportunity to review the audio recordings of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is an accurate -- that audio recording is -- is an accurate representation of your evidence at that time?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If are you asked today about the matters that you testified to in the Brdjanin case, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber, and that is, even if you couldn't formulate it in exactly the same answers, the essence would be the same?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender 09 -- sorry, 90273, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours leave, I will now read a short summary. The witness, Grgo Stojic, was born and grew up in the village of Skrljevita in the Sanski Most municipality. He lived there until 1992 at which time he was 24 years of age. The witness testified regarding the general situation in the Sanski Most municipality, the check-points, the restriction of movement and the demands made by the Sanski Most Crisis Staff over the radio ordering non-Serbs to surrender their weapons. The witness primarily testified about the killing of a number of men of Croat ethnicity near the village of Skrljevita in the Sanski Most municipality on or about the 2nd of November, 1992. He is the sole survivor of this incident. On that day, he and his cousin were ambushed by the two persons of Serb ethnicity, one of whom he came to know as Danilusko Kajtez. The two Serbs ordered the witness and his cousin to follow them. They were taken a short distance to where four Croat neighbours were being detained by another two persons of Serb ethnicity. The six Croat men were ordered to line up. They were searched, questioned, and personal belongings seized. They were all beaten with truncheons. They were then shot. The witness was shot in his left upper arm and he fell straight to the ground. As he was lying on the ground, he felt a bullet hit his hip and exist through his stomach. When the witness got up, he realized all the other men were dead. One of the five men had his skull blown to bits. The witness managed to make his way to his village and was eventually taken to the Sanski Most health centre. He was then transferred to Prijedor and then to the Banja Luka hospital where he was operated on. On the 9th of November, he was moved from the intensive care unit to a room in the urology unit referred to by the witness as a prison cell. Between 9 November and the time he was released, which was 11 December 1992, he did not receive regular medical treatment. Hospital staff allowed other patients and civilians and soldiers to beat the witness and other patients kept in the same room as he on a number of occasions. They were kicked and punched and beaten. The witness was kicked in the stomach until he started bleeding. Upon his release, he spent three days at Caritas before being take to Croatia. That completes the summary of the witness's evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I have a couple of questions for you. You testified that after you left the Banja Luka hospital, you spent a few days with Caritas before being taken to Croatia. How were you transported to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to Croatia in a Caritas convoy from Banja Luka to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified that you suffered gun-shot wounds to your hip and stomach and upper arm on the 2nd of November, 1992. In late 1994, did you undergo a bone transplant in hospital in the United States --

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- to try and give you more function with your left arm?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 65 ter 16820A, please. Is the photo in e-court? Are we able to turn it -- turn it around?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, are these two photographs contained within a medical journal article published in the United States which you provided to the OTP in 2001?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The photograph on the left was taken in 1994 just before your surgery, and the photograph on the right was taken in November 1994, after your surgery; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... your treating physician, Dr. Rayan, on the right in that photograph, the photograph on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Besides having to live with your arm like that for two years before the surgery, what other physical or psychological effects did you or do you suffer as a consequence of what you experienced in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: To this very day, I have nightmares, fear that still remains. It's difficult to live as a disabled person with a 70 per cent permanent disability needing the help of others without enough financial means to live, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we deal with the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to a number of exhibits which were shown to the witness at page 6793 and -94 of his transcript, there's about six or maybe seven of them. I don't know that those were sufficiently discussed with the witness so that they form an integral part of his testimony. In addition, they don't seem appropriate for admission through this witness. They are essentially records of the court case of Danilusko Kajtez. And this witness was not a participant in that case, and it all happened after he left Bosnia. And he really doesn't give any information. In fact, some of those documents were never even shown to him. They were just simply mentioned by the Prosecutor. So for 65 ters numbers 5657, 5706, 17750, 20560, 20562, 20588, and 20592, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not seek to tender 5657, 17750. 20562 was discussed with the witness, and also in cross-examination the document was shown to the witness at transcript page 6801. And also 20560 was also shown in cross-examination at transcript page 6801. And I would seek not to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last one, the 65 ter number of the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then I would not seek to tender 20592, 20588, and 05706. They can -- those five exhibits can come in through another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are tendering, among those seven, only two.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 20560, 20562, which was also discussed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber, those two documents form an indispensable and inseparable part of the transcript and on that basis we admit them. And the others -- together with the others, those will be given numbers in due course and informed to the parties. But there's one matter for the Court Deputy to clarify with respect to the exhibit number. Ms. Sutherland, you are minded to tendered that -- the photo we saw?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that would be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P3516, Your Honours. And just to clarify a change in the exhibit numbering. On the last hearing date, on the 30th of September, two 65 ter numbers, 849A and 848, were admitted as P3516 MFI and P3517 MFI. The exhibits will now be changed to read as follows: 65 ter number 849A will be Exhibit P3511, and 65 ter number 848 will be Exhibit P3514, both marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before Mr. Karadzic begins his cross-examination, Mr. Tieger, I just heard from the Court Deputy before I entered the courtroom that there was a change of witnesses' order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, necessitated by the subpoena issue and the lack of progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could it not have been informed earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we kept the Defence -- as I was in fairly regular contact with Mr. Robinson. And the problem, Mr. President, is that there was no definitive word one way or another. So we made our best efforts to be as conversant with the status of the situation as possible, but even at the -- and as I explained to Mr. Robinson, even at what was nearly the last minute we were still uncertain about where we stood, and that's about the best I could do. So we didn't have a definitive change, and that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I don't recall whether or not there were -- I assumed the Registry was as alert to that. And I -- we can develop a protocol, of course, for similar contact with Chamber's personnel as we know these things. We're not really aware of the extent to which there's communication between the Registry and Chamber's personnel about issues such as that. But we'd be more than happy to discuss the best mode of communication under circumstances such as the one we faced toward the end of last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what's the witnesses' order like as it stands now for the remainder of the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, what we've discussed is proceeding in the order we had listed. I understand that there's one matter that the Defence wishes to raise in connection with that. But that is what we discussed with Mr. Robinson at the end of the week and over the course of the weekend, and that's still our intention. There are a couple of wrinkles with that. One of which is, as I mentioned, I think will be raised by the Defence, and there's a minor one to be raised on behalf of the Prosecution as well, but that's our intention at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we are not sure when we will be hearing the witness who was the subject of subpoena.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. And it's a matter I raised with the Registry as well. Depending on -- I mean, that raises a further scheduling issue that should be discussed. I still don't know what the anticipated date of service is at this point, but given the Court schedule, we certainly want to consider the advisability of bringing the witness, should he be served, later in the week, and we might want to consider a different time for travel. So the service is fine, but then we may want to liaise with VWU to determine whether the witness is to be brought forthwith or his date of travel should be extended to a time that conforms a little bit better to the current schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So I'll take that you will pay your utmost care so that the parties and Chamber could be properly informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We certainly will, Your Honour. And, as I said, we've had regular contact with the Defence and kept them as up-to-date as we have been, and we've made considerable proactive efforts to be as alert -- as aware as possible about what was happening in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Stojic. Your testimony in the case of Brdjanin was admitted in lieu of your examination-in-chief. Now you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to express my solidarity because of your wounds because of all of the suffering that you experienced. Because that photograph is the freshest image, I would like to ask you this: Why was this surgery not carried out in Croatia? Why did you have to go to America?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Because there was a long waiting-list. I didn't get my turn. And I also didn't have money to pay for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that in America it was cheaper than in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I travelled through the international immigration organisation, IOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was supposed to have been done in Croatia, could this have been done in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could have been done, but I didn't have the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you went to the market. Are you trying to say that at the time the market was working, operating in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what did you take to the market and how often?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Some agricultural products so that we could get salt for that, coffee, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often did you go to the market?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't go very often. The market day was on Mondays.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you went on Mondays. And tell me, is it correct that it was possible to go until the first attack, the first fighting in Sanski Most, until late May -- in late May?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure that I put a precise question. Moving around in the municipality was free and possible until the first attack in late May, the 25th, the 26th, and the 27th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then after the fighting there was a request to hand over weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that this was announced over the Serbian radio in Sanski Most, but it was not said that the weapons are to be handed over by specific ethnic groups but that weapons should be handed over?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard on Radio Sanski Most that this related or concerned the villages of Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any weapons there?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Some did have legal weapons and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any weapons in your village?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: People who had weapons with a permit, they possessed them legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And a number of those weapons were handed over; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the Serbs had information that there were still 86 rifles which had been obtained from Croatia which were not handed over; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, these were just stories. It was just talk. None of the Croats received that many rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, then you needed to have permission to be able to move around, passes?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is something that those who did not fight accepted as part of normal procedure during the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you feel safer with a pass in your pocket; and was this pass something that allowed you to pass through?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the pass actually wasn't valid. It was worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you and me to pause between question and answer because of the translation. Is it true that the authorities in Sanski Most offered the option to civilians to go somewhere if they wanted to go somewhere; and for those who wanted to stay, the authorities did everything they could to provide guarantees for those who stayed?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They did promise and provide guarantees, but this was not actually respected. It didn't go the way it was supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We will come to those who violated that. Your family applied to leave somewhere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I also was requesting documents in order to be able to leave. Unfortunately, I wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it difficult to obtain the documents? What documents were required exactly?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you needed a lot. You needed to sign out. You needed to pay some fees. I can't remember exactly what -- how much. It's been 19 years since then. You needed passes and so on and so forth. I cannot remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it necessary to have some good connections in order to get yourself on the list for the convoy?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything of the sort. The only thing that mattered was to have money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To pay your taxes, to produce a receipt accordingly, and to pay for the papers to be issued to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have to pay any fares?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I did not pay any transportation fares because I was already in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you if you knew many people who left in convoys.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. Those people were charged up to 170 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How -- what about those who didn't have any money? They couldn't go?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately there were quite a few people who remained behind. They perished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at this mechanism. First you apply to go, then they give you a list of various certificates and documents that you have to provide?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation, and I'm asking you to do the same. And after that, if you have any outstanding tax, you pay it, and you get yourself on a convoy list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you are notified about the next convoy; right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how they notified us. But I myself was transferred from the hospital to a prison in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that later. I'm just asking you, had this not happened, you would have been waiting for the convoy and just waiting for the notification about the convoy. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How were you notified? On the radio, by post, by personal contacts?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the absence of any convoys, you stayed in your village up until the 2nd of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that you went to Sanski Most only on Mondays, because that was the market day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that in order for you to sell your produce you needed the money from that to buy other items from the shops. What was the situation with how items were available?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some staple items available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the school working in your area?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, when Tomo Potalac [phoen] went on that day to Sanski Most to fetch some textbooks, he was killed on the way and that was the day when I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was the school located?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: In my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you remember that the academic year ended somewhat earlier in mid-May but it had started more or less at -- on time in September?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the name of your school?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It was the Hasan Kikic elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that an independent school or was it a part of the education system of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It was a branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the main school was in Sanski Most and it was called Hasan Kikic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber who Hasan Kikic was, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was a literary author.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity? And am I right if I say that he was a revolutionary, a Communist?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't go into the matter of his ethnicity. But as far as I can remember, he should have been a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the teacher in your village?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: A woman of Serb ethnicity by the name of Nada.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Later on you mentioned her as having helped you about something in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 2nd of November you set off as usual, because supposedly it was a Monday, and you headed off towards the market; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On those market days in Sanski Most, were there more people than usual?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Of course. There was a bigger crowd on every market day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time there were no restrictions, with the exception of check-points and checks made at those check-points; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You went to Sanski Most, you sold your produce, you went to the shops to buy whatever you needed, and then you headed back home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were crossing the bridge on the little stream in Harkusa [phoen] you noticed two criminals behind a bush. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You described this unfortunate event, and it struck me that these two people identified themselves to you as member of some kind of paramilitary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They did not -- or, actually, what did they wear? What did they have on their heads? What insignia did they wear?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: One of them was dressed as a military policeman. He had a submachine-gun. He had a military cap and a badge. The other one was in civilian clothes. He had a leather jacket and also a submachine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And one of them had a sort of cockade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You immediately realized that those were paramilitaries and that, by definition, you knew that they were beyond any civilian or military command or control?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't realize that those were paramilitaries. But when we were brought to the four men who had already been captured before me, that's when I realized that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you certainly knew that paramilitaries were under nobody's control, and that is what you said in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That was clear to me, and that was how it should be in a normal --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But at that point you didn't know who they were. You didn't know their names.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later on, an inspector questioned you whether those men were -- actually one of those men was Kajtez, and he asked you to describe him.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was one in the civilian clothes; right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please just pause between questions and answers. As for the one who had cockade on his hat was a man by the name of Vukojevic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Supposedly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You immediately saw that they were criminals.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, not immediately. I didn't realize they were criminals. It only occurred to me when they searched us before shooting us, and they told us that they were members of Seselj's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in your statement of 10th February 1993, 65 ter 22616, you said that you noticed two criminals behind a bush; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were criminals, but they were armed with military-issue weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, then, can we agree that in our region there was no other types of weapons available?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the criminals always find their way around when it comes to procuring weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that they lined you up and fired at you; right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But before that, they confiscated all the means we had, including money. They searched us. They lined us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think that it would have been more lucrative for them to wait until you were coming back from the market, that you would have had more money on you? Was the money the motive?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you took the same route to and from the market?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you didn't see exactly who fired?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't do that because I had my back turned on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on in your statements and testimonies you described in detail how you managed to get through and get some medical aid. First you came to some houses, and then you were driven in a car to the medical centre in Sanski Most. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had to go through Gornji Kruhari and Koljak?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on that road all the way to Sanski Most nobody stopped you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you lying in the car, as a wounded person would normally do?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The police stopped you in the centre of Sanski Most, asked what happened, and you kindly explained to them, and they kindly directed you to the medical centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were admitted immediately in Sanski Most. They stopped the bleeding. They gave you first aid and asked you about what had happened. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As soon as you reached the medical centre, the doctors came out, they put you on a stretcher, they took you to an A and E room, and that is where the bleeding was stopped.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were still bleeding at that point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh, thank you. Since you have lost a lot of blood, you must have been exhausted?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then the police arrived and took your statement, in which you explained in great detail about what had transpired.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statements, you say that the policemen were polite and fair and caused no problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They themselves told you that that was a group that was operating independently.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So after they stopped the bleeding, you were immediately transferred to Prijedor. Is there a bigger hospital in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The hospital in Prijedor is for treatment, whereas in Sanski Most it's only a medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's a lower level of medical care.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They gave you their ambulance and it took you to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were escorted by a policeman whilst in the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He accompanied you because there could have been extremists on the road and you would have been safer to have a policeman by your side.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were immediately admitted at Prijedor hospital at 10.00. Risto Stojanovski examined you and said immediately that he has to make a referral to Banja Luka because he was not able to treat you.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It took you half an hour to reach Banja Luka, and in the next half-hour you found yourself on the operation table; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And between the period when you were wounded until such time that you underwent surgery, you didn't have any criticism with regard to either doctors or the authorities. However, the first problems occurred after the surgery; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today, in examination-in-chief, it was mentioned that some people were beaten, that some people were brazen and arrogant. In your statement you said that some people were enraged, but you said the medical staff, the nurses and the doctors, were caring and brought you food.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Only two nurses were treating me in a fair way, but that happened only after I had been put into a cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were still in the hospital but in a ward that was kept under guard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It would be helpful to establish who were these individuals who harassed you, what the specific circumstances and reasons were. In your evidence in Brdjanin, at page -- that's 65 ter 92 -- 90293, I think it has a P, at page 6788 and 6789, you talk about these events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, can we have page 6788. 65 ter 90273. It's the last P.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P3515.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see line 23 on this page? I'll read it for you. This was the question: [In English] [As read] "What about the people who were with you in the cell, how were they treated? "A. Counsel, I know that Ramiz Skoric who was killed in Manjaca, who was wounded in Manjaca, he lost both legs. He said that Manjaca was great and that he was happy about the fact that we were going to be transferred to Manjaca camp. So when they were taken away for questioning, that's why there were told -- that's what they were told."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English. Of the transcript, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Q. Mr. Stojic, you said you were beaten more than one time. What about the people who were in the cell with you? "A. Yes. "Q. Were they beaten? "A. Yes, they beat everyone. While they were beating the people in cell number 8, we would hear terrible blows. We were already started getting ready in cell number 9 in order to get through this more easily. "Q. Who did the beating? "A. We were beaten by civilians and by soldiers and by anyone who could enter that cell. "Q. When you are referring to soldiers, can you be more specific? What kind of soldiers? "A. Serbian soldiers. "Q. Can you be more specific? Were they regular reservists, military police? "A. Who knows what they were like. I think they were the ones who were sent away who weren't under control. They were out of control." [Interpretation] Thank you. Who sent them away?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last answer, lines 21 and 22, you say: [In English] "I think they were the ones who were send away who weren't under control." [Interpretation] Who sent them away?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: How should I know? There was a guard for the two cells. The doorknob had been pulled out of the door. And when the soldier who stood guard had to open the door, he would insert the doorknob, open the door, and then let the person in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what did you mean when you said that they were sent away? Where were they sent away from and who sent them?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this is what you said, and I wanted to clarify this bit. You also say that Nurse Ljubislava [phoen] did not behave professionally, whereas the others did and they brought you food.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: If she was not unprofessional or not, I don't know about that. But I do know that she was brazen and impolite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I'll read out how you answered in the trial against Mr. Brdjanin. The question was like this: "Can you be even more specific? Were they regular reservists, military police?" You were talking about the -- those who beat you at the cell. And your answer is like this: "Who knows what they were like. I think they were the ones who were sent away ..." Do you remember what you meant by saying "the ones who were sent away"?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Whenever the guard would open the door, whoever wanted to step into the cell, be it a civilian or a soldier, could do so. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as you personally are concerned, you were exposed to these physical harassments on two occasions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On one occasion it was a drunkard who beat you, from Uzice; right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the second time was when you were slapped about by a guard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's right. But he also beat me in the stomach, the one that I mentioned earlier, the soldier who entered the cell. He kicked me with his military boot.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look 65 ter 22618 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your other statement. This is a 2000 statement. It's 65 ter 22618. Page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at that page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the fourth paragraph, which reads: "The first time I was beat up was by a person from the street who was drunk and he called me a Ustasha." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he wasn't a soldier. He was just a person, a hobo, if you will, who was drunk?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I did say that everyone was allowed admittance there. Whoever wanted to gain entrances, be it a man, a woman, soldier, or civilian, they would be let through by the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he called you by a derogatory term, the Ustasha. Is that how you understood it?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a derogatory term. When I -- this happened right after I was transferred from the surgery room down to the ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this was the prison ward of the hospital where people were brought over from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about others being brought in from the outside. I know that those of us who happened to be in the hospital and who were not Serbs were taken to that ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am a bit puzzled by the letter sent by Bishop Komarica related to your stay at the hospital. That's 16817, 65 ter document. Where did Bishop Komarica get the information about you being in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he got that information from. I do remember, though, that when I was released from detention I was given a letter and a visa in order to cross over into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But somebody did let him know that you were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's right. But I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In his letter, he stated that as of the 2nd of November up until the 11th of December you were in the hospital and not in prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: He may have worded it that way. But as of the 9th of November I was in a prison cell, up until the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's clear this matter up. Is this a section of the hospital under guard?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It is part of the hospital. It was on the urological ward. And the prison cells were in rooms 8 and 9, hospital rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the Brdjanin transcript on our screens again. Page 6808. Well, yes, this is Bishop Komarica's letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was a bishop in Banja Luka, was he not?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you left the hospital, you were taken to the Catholic charity organisation, Caritas, which existed with this parish; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have the Brdjanin transcript, page 6808.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this part of your evidence, you're discussing the issue, whether this was a hospital or a prison. Based on the document that was shown to you, you were in a hospital. And in line 21, you say: [In English] [As read] "On the basis of this document, where you can see all three men were in hospital in Banja Luka, and their lives were endangered because the witnesses were inconvenient -- are inconvenient witnesses to crime in the municipality of Sanski Most. The above-named people are from Skrljevita municipality of Sanski Most." [Interpretation] So the document which was shown to you read that you were inconvenient witnesses to crimes in Sanski Most. And was it clear to you that this was the basis on which you were held, and was it possible for a criminal also from Sanski Most to get into that part of the hospital where you were held to cause you harm?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how am I able to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's read on. The signature says - and if we can have the next page. [In English] "If that's a hospital in normal conditions, as it should be according to the conventions of the International Committee of the Red Cross, then I -- in such a case, our lives would not have been in danger. "Q. I'm not arguing the conditions that may have prevailed in that hospital, but my only question was were you in the hospital itself and not in a prison of Tunjice, at least on the basis of this document? "A. I was in urology ward in hospital, in cell number 9. First of all, I was in cell number 8." [Interpretation] Therefore, it follows from your answer that you were aware of the fact that you were held there as a witness and not as a criminal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. I don't know if I was held there as a witness. I know that I had never been a criminal, and I hope that I will never be one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon your release from the hospital on the 11th of December, and until the 14th of December, you must have been somewhere. You must have spent these two or three days somewhere. Where was it?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: In the Caritas offices in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These were offices belonging to the church, because it is a religious charity organisation, Caritas. Did you go to church during that period?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's in the very heart of Banja Luka, is it not?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the very centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see how you went on to describe the arrival of inspectors to -- of the inspector to the Banja Luka hospital when you gave a statement to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we have transcript page 6899 of this -- 6799 of this same document. Thank you. 6799, line 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "And afterwards, at the Banja Luka hospital, this other inspector, Mile Dosen, that you mentioned today, he also arrived, didn't he? "A. Yes, he did. "Q. And you told him, too, exactly what happened? "A. Yes, I did. That's right." [Interpretation] Is it true that Mile Dosen told you, after having questioned you, that you should not worry and that everything would be fine?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That's true. That's what he told me. But he said that while I was still upstairs in the surgical ward, before I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. He asked you about the killing of all of those Croats, and he asked you if you knew Dane Kajtez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Dane Kajtez or did he suggest to you that that could have been him and asked you to describe him?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, he did talk about him and describe him to me, and he asked me if he was wearing a leather jacket. I confirmed that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then he asked you what he looked like, and so on, so that you would be able to confirm or deny that it was this particular person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that after the statement to Inspector Dosen an indictment was issued against Kajtez and his associates, his co-perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I did hear that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But soon after, you left the territory of Republika Srpska and you did not have direct information about what was going on regarding the trial of Kajtez and others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in that period from 1993 to 1995, you didn't see Kajtez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, how could I have seen him when I wasn't even in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were the only person who survived that incident; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So can we then say that you were a valuable eye-witness, as far as the court authorities were concerned?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you were absent for a long time as the chief witness, and you were not available to them at that time.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And had they called you before the peace was signed to come and testify, would you have done that?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I have told already this Court that I wouldn't have, but I went back on my word and I went in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask the question and I said after the peace was signed, because, of course, you would have been afraid and cautious about moving around. At the time, there were no diplomatic relations between Republika Srpska and the Republic of Croatia; is that right.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that at the time the post wasn't working and it wasn't easy to send a letter directly to Croatia, or a parcel?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This page -- the same document, but can we now look at page 6810-- 001. And can you please look at line 2. I'm going to read in English so that it can be translated correctly. [In English] [As read] "Do you know whether there were any diplomatic relations or any other relations between Croatia and Republika Srpska or whether the postal services functioned between Republika Srpska and Croatia? "A. The postal services did not function, but there were humanitarian organisations that were functioning. "Q. When you came to Croatia, did you send your address to Republika Srpska? "A. To whom would I do that?" [Interpretation] The police organs in Republika Srpska at the time did not have your new address in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, once again, I would like to express my sympathies and my solidarity to you. I don't have any more questions, since the -- the statements have not been tendered or admitted, and I would ask you to accept that I am completely on your side and that I wish you the very best in your path to recovery. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your words are touching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, just one question. Mr. Karadzic asked -- put it to you whether you were detained in the Banja Luka hospital as a prisoner or a witness, and you said that -- or he put to you that you could possibly be -- have been detained there as a witness, and you said you don't know that. Do you recall that question and answer?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I do. Unfortunately, I was not detained as a witness, but as a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 16823, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, is this a copy of your medical discharge letter that you received from the Banja Luka hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to the top of the -- the top of the page, we can see something has been whited out in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of this document in e-court. And if we can blow up the top left-hand corner, the writing in the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What does that writing say? Are you able to read that, Mr. Stojic, which is on the -- written on the -- the front of this discharge form?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It says "zarob," which is abbreviated for "zarobljen," "captured."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you -- did you know who wrote that notation on the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote that. Probably the staff in the hospital, in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So it was on the top of the document when you received this discharge form?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to read that. I don't read that like that. I cannot read it like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, why is this page the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's also the correct way, Your Honour. But if --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, do you have the original of that document that you provided the other day?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I do have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stojic provided the original document, and it was rescanned on both ways. The front -- on the front of the document, it's white-painted out. But if you turn the document over, you can actually see what's written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doesn't -- does the Defence wish to examine the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you take the document from the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson. Could the usher bring the document to the Bench first. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, with all due respect, I am a doctor, and I am familiar with these discharge papers. This here at the top in no way can be an integral part of this medical document; is that right? Because what the doctor had to write, he wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not a proper question. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, do you know who wrote this part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I don't know. This is the discharge paper or document that I received, like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you know who white-painted this part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that either, because that's how I received the discharge document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would just like to ask Mr. Stojic whether this part that was filled in by the doctor and signed by him, does it say anywhere that you were in prison?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, at the top corner it says "zarob," which is abbreviated for "zarobljen," "captured," and then this has been whited out. And I have documents from the International Committee of the Red Cross that I was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But other than this handwritten and erased part, does it not say that this is surgery, the urology department, all of the work was described, there was a lot of things that were done in the area of the stomach and the hand, and that's described in detail; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it you're tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I would seek to have the translation revised, because it refers in the translation to the witness's right arm and I want the interpreters to translate - the translators, I'm sorry - to check that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ratari sinistri [phoen], in Latin it states, would be the left hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take your word that this will be revised. With that understanding, we'll admit it in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P3527, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. That concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague again to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. We'll rise all together. We'll have a break till 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Then the witness can be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to the next proposed Prosecution witness, we're not in a position to be able to cross-examine him today because of the lack of notice that we had that he would be testifying. The Prosecution did do a very good job of trying to deal with a very difficult situation, and they did, at the end of Friday, tell us that there was some potential that Mr. Tupajic would not be present but that they were trying to get him here. So we prepared for Mr. Tupajic. And then on Friday evening, at 4.45, we did receive for the first time an amalgamated statement of Mr. Mesanovic. But we didn't have time to prepare for the cross-examination of Mr. Mesanovic, and in fact Dr. Karadzic hasn't even brought to court with him any of the materials for that witness. So we propose, if the Chamber would be willing, that we hear whatever direct examination that's offered by the Prosecution and then tomorrow morning we have the cross-examination of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just note, Mr. President, I -- I -- well, the simple thing I want to know is that if the Court is inclined to grant the request, then I would not suggest we move forward to hear the extremely limited time that would be involved in direct examination. In fact, one of the wrinkles I was going to mention is that Ms. Sutherland needs to check with the witness over the break because of the accelerated nature of his arrival and efforts to complete review of the material as to whether or not there was going to be a slight delay involved in moving him forward. So if the Court is going to grant the request, then I think there's no -- no point in moving forward on his testimony today in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the circumstances, the Chamber is minded to grant the Defence motion. But before we adjourn, I will issue an oral ruling with regard to the accused's motion to -- motion for reclassification of ex parte filing with respect to Witness KDZ532, filed on 28th of September, 2011. The Chamber notes the Prosecution's response filed on 29th of September, 2011, not opposing the motion. The Chamber hereby grants the motion and orders that the confidential and ex parte Appendix D to the Prosecution's motion for delayed disclosure for KDZ456, KDZ493, KDZ532, and KDZ531, and variation of protective measures for KDZ489, filed on 8th of May, 2009, be disclosed to the accused and reclassified as confidential. Unless there are any matters to be raised, the hearing is now adjourned. And we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of October, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.31 a.m.,
